claim: Cohesin is required for sister chromatid cohesion in yeast cells.
source: In yeast cells, cohesin is not only required for sister chromatid cohesion but also plays a major role determining the structure of individual chromatids in metaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about cohesin function.

claim: Cohesin plays a major role determining the structure of individual chromatids in metaphase in yeast cells.
source: In yeast cells, cohesin is not only required for sister chromatid cohesion but also plays a major role determining the structure of individual chromatids in metaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cited literature.

claim: Separase cleavage is thought to remove all cohesin complexes from chromosomes to initiate anaphase.
source: Separase cleavage is thought to remove all cohesin complexes from chromosomes to initiate anaphase.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field that the manuscript challenges.

claim: Degradation of cohesin at the anaphase onset causes aberrant chromatid segregation.
source: Here, we show that degradation of cohesin at the anaphase onset causes aberrant chromatid segregation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cohesin depletion causes loss of intrachromatid organisation during anaphase.
source: Hi-C analysis on segregating chromatids demonstrates that cohesin depletion causes loss of intrachromatid organisation.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data presented in Figure 4.

claim: TEV-mediated cleavage of cohesin does not dramatically disrupt chromatid organisation in anaphase.
source: Surprisingly, tobacco etch virus (TEV)-mediated cleavage of cohesin does not dramatically disrupt chromatid organisation in anaphase, explaining why bulk segregation is achieved.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis shown in Figure 4 and segregation data in Figure 3.

claim: A small pool of cohesin complexes is bound to telophase chromosomes in wild-type cells.
source: In addition, we identified a small pool of cohesin complexes bound to telophase chromosomes in wild-type cells and show that they play a role in the organisation of centromeric regions.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5 and microscopy in Figure 5a.

claim: Cohesin complexes bound to telophase chromosomes play a role in the organisation of centromeric regions.
source: In addition, we identified a small pool of cohesin complexes bound to telophase chromosomes in wild-type cells and show that they play a role in the organisation of centromeric regions.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis in Figure 6 showing changes in centromeric organization upon cohesin depletion.

claim: In yeast cells cohesin function extends to the anaphase period when chromatids are segregating.
source: Our data demonstrates that in yeast cells cohesin function is not over in metaphase, but extends to the anaphase period when chromatids are segregating.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Cohesin holds sister chromatids together.
source: Cohesin is a multisubunit protein complex that holds sister chromatids together (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997) and promotes condensation of metaphase chromosomes (Guacci et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guacci et al., 1997 and Michaelis et al., 1997.

claim: Cohesin promotes condensation of metaphase chromosomes.
source: Cohesin is a multisubunit protein complex that holds sister chromatids together (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997) and promotes condensation of metaphase chromosomes (Guacci et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guacci et al., 1997.

claim: The core proteins of cohesin are Smc1, Smc3, and Mcd1/Scc1.
source: The core proteins of cohesin are a pair of structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) proteins, Smc1 and Smc3, and the conserved kleisin factor Mcd1/Scc1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cohesin composition.

claim: Cohesin forms a tripartite complex with a rod-shaped structure.
source: Together they form a tripartite complex that has a rod-shaped structure (Bürmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bürmann et al., 2019.

claim: Cohesin complexes contain the HEAT-repeat proteins Scc3 and Pds5.
source: Cohesin complexes also contain the HEAT-repeat proteins Scc3 and Pds5 (Hartman et al., 2000; Losada et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hartman et al., 2000 and Losada et al., 2000.

claim: Cohesin organises chromosomes through the formation of chromatin loops in interphase nuclei.
source: In addition to its role in sister chromatid cohesion, studies have shown that cohesin also organises chromosomes through the formation of chromatin loops in interphase nuclei (Rao et al., 2017) and mitotic chromatids (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rao et al., 2017.

claim: Cohesin organises chromosomes through the formation of chromatin loops in mitotic chromatids.
source: In addition to its role in sister chromatid cohesion, studies have shown that cohesin also organises chromosomes through the formation of chromatin loops in interphase nuclei (Rao et al., 2017) and mitotic chromatids (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017 and Schalbetter et al., 2017.

claim: The role of cohesin in nuclear organisation is thought to depend on its ability to extrude DNA loops.
source: The role of cohesin in nuclear organisation is thought to depend on its ability to extrude DNA loops, an activity that was recently confirmed in vitro with human cohesin (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2019 and Kim et al., 2019.

claim: Separase cleaves cohesin's kleisin Mcd1 subunit in mitosis.
source: Separase cleaves cohesin's kleisin Mcd1/Rad21/Scc1 subunit (thereafter referred to as Mcd1) in mitosis (Uhlmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uhlmann et al., 1999.

claim: Engineered Mcd1 cleavage in metaphase using TEV protease triggers bulk separation of the genome.
source: Engineered Mcd1 cleavage in metaphase, using TEV protease expression and TEV recognition sites in Mcd1, triggers bulk separation of the genome (Uhlmann et al., 2000), demonstrating that one of cohesin's functions is to hold sister chromatids together prior to their separation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uhlmann et al., 2000.

claim: Cohesin mediates intrachromosomal loops that are responsible for compacting yeast chromosome arms in metaphase cells.
source: Recent work using chromosome capture (Hi-C) techniques has demonstrated that cohesin mediates intrachromosomal loops that are responsible for compacting yeast chromosome arms in metaphase cells, independently of cohesin's role in sister chromatid cohesion (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017 and Schalbetter et al., 2017.

claim: Cohesin is responsible for the organisation of the genome into loops during interphase in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells cohesin is responsible for the organisation of the genome into loops during interphase (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rao et al., 2017.

claim: During prophase the bulk of cohesin dissociates from chromosome arms in mammalian cells.
source: During prophase the bulk of cohesin dissociates from chromosome arms (Sumara et al., 2000), however since sister chromatids remain paired, it is likely that some cohesin complexes are retained on chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sumara et al., 2000.

claim: At metaphase, mammalian cohesin is mainly localised to centromeres where it provides cohesion.
source: At metaphase, mammalian cohesin is mainly localised to centromeres where it provides cohesion (Sumara et al., 2000), while the related SMC complexes, condensin I and II (CI and CII), take over the role of folding mitotic chromosome arms into loops (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sumara et al., 2000.

claim: Condensin I and II take over the role of folding mitotic chromosome arms into loops in mammalian cells.
source: At metaphase, mammalian cohesin is mainly localised to centromeres where it provides cohesion (Sumara et al., 2000), while the related SMC complexes, condensin I and II (CI and CII), take over the role of folding mitotic chromosome arms into loops (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gibcus et al., 2018.

claim: Condensin II organises large (200–400 kb) loops in mammalian cells.
source: CII organises large (200–400 kb) loops, while CI sub-divides these into smaller loops (80 kb) (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gibcus et al., 2018.

claim: Condensin I sub-divides large loops into smaller loops (80 kb) in mammalian cells.
source: CII organises large (200–400 kb) loops, while CI sub-divides these into smaller loops (80 kb) (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gibcus et al., 2018.

claim: During interphase, condensin I is excluded from the nucleus in mammalian cells.
source: During interphase CI is excluded from the nucleus and CII, although nuclear, is prevented from acting on chromosomal DNAs by a nuclear protein, Mcph1 (Yamashita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamashita et al., 2011.

claim: During interphase, condensin II is prevented from acting on chromosomal DNAs by Mcph1 in mammalian cells.
source: During interphase CI is excluded from the nucleus and CII, although nuclear, is prevented from acting on chromosomal DNAs by a nuclear protein, Mcph1 (Yamashita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamashita et al., 2011.

claim: A rapid switch from condensin binding to cohesin binding between anaphase and cytokinesis has been reported in mammalian cells.
source: Interestingly, a rapid switch from condensin binding to cohesin binding between anaphase and cytokinesis has been reported (Abramo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abramo et al., 2019.

claim: Yeast cells lack a condensin II complex.
source: Yeast cells lack a CII complex, and CI role in chromosome organisation in mitosis is restricted to the ribosomal gene array (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about yeast biology.

claim: Condensin I role in chromosome organisation in mitosis is restricted to the ribosomal gene array in yeast.
source: Yeast cells lack a CII complex, and CI role in chromosome organisation in mitosis is restricted to the ribosomal gene array (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017 and Schalbetter et al., 2017.

claim: Yeast condensin is involved in the separation of chromosome arms through a role that promotes decatenation of sister chromatids.
source: Instead, yeast condensin is involved in the separation of chromosome arms (Leonard et al., 2015) through a role that promotes decatenation of sister chromatids (Baxter et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leonard et al., 2015, Baxter et al., 2011, and Sen et al., 2016.

claim: Full degradation of Mcd1-aid occurs 30–60 min after addition of auxin in cdc20-arrested cells.
source: In cdc20-arrested cells, we observed full degradation of Mcd1-aid 30–60 min after addition of auxin (Figure 1a), demonstrating the rapid and efficient removal of Mcd1 in this experimental setup.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1 in cdc20-arrested cells precipitates an anaphase-like stage.
source: Like TEV-induced anaphases, auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1 in cdc20-arrested cells precipitates an anaphase-like stage (Figure 1b), however we observed severe disruption of nuclear segregation (Figure 1b), with many nuclei appearing to be stuck in anaphase with elongated nuclear masses for extended periods (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Figure 1b.

claim: Auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1 causes severe disruption of nuclear segregation.
source: Like TEV-induced anaphases, auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1 in cdc20-arrested cells precipitates an anaphase-like stage (Figure 1b), however we observed severe disruption of nuclear segregation (Figure 1b), with many nuclei appearing to be stuck in anaphase with elongated nuclear masses for extended periods (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Figure 1b-c.

claim: After 180 min of auxin addition to cdc20-blocked cultures, 48% of cells were still stuck in anaphase.
source: After 180 min of auxin addition to cdc20-blocked cultures, we observed that 48% of the cells were still stuck in anaphase (Figure 1c), 35% of cells showed correct segregation of arm tags, and 20% showed missegregation (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: After 180 min of auxin addition to cdc20-blocked cultures, 35% of cells showed correct segregation of arm tags on chromosome 5.
source: After 180 min of auxin addition to cdc20-blocked cultures, we observed that 48% of the cells were still stuck in anaphase (Figure 1c), 35% of cells showed correct segregation of arm tags, and 20% showed missegregation (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: After 180 min of auxin addition to cdc20-blocked cultures, 20% of cells showed missegregation of arm tags on chromosome 5.
source: After 180 min of auxin addition to cdc20-blocked cultures, we observed that 48% of the cells were still stuck in anaphase (Figure 1c), 35% of cells showed correct segregation of arm tags, and 20% showed missegregation (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Segregation errors were higher for telomeric regions than for arm regions of chromosome 5 after Mcd1 degradation.
source: Segregation errors were even higher for telomeric regions (Figure 1d) and larger chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of data in Figure 1c and Figure 1d.

claim: Rapid removal of Mcd1 by degradation causes an anaphase-like state with impaired separation of chromatids.
source: These results demonstrate that rapid removal of Mcd1 by degradation causes an anaphase-like state with impaired separation of chromatids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Induction of TEV expression led to cleavage of Mcd1 after 60 min.
source: Induction of TEV expression led to cleavage of Mcd1 after 60 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) as expected.
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bulk nuclear segregation occurred 90–120 min following TEV induction.
source: Bulk nuclear segregation occurred 90–120 min following the induction as it had been previously reported (Uhlmann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is observed in the current study and consistent with previous reports.

claim: Chromosome tags located on the centromere region of chromosome 5 segregated efficiently in TEV-induced anaphases.
source: Importantly, chromosome tags located on the centromere region of chromosome 5 segregated efficiently (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TEV cleavage allows nuclear segregation unlike auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1.
source: Therefore, unlike auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1, and consistent with previous reports (Uhlmann et al., 2000), TEV cleavage allows nuclear segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cleaved C-terminal fragment of Mcd1 was fully stable during the entire timecourse in TEV-induced anaphases.
source: We noticed that in TEV-induced anaphases, the cleaved C-terminal fragment of Mcd1 was fully stable during the entire timecourse (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TEV protease cleavage leaves a glycine residue at the N-termini which is not well recognised by the N-rule pathway.
source: The lack of Mcd1 fragment degradation after TEV cleavage stems from the fact that TEV protease cleavage occurs following the glutamine (Q) residue of the TEV recognition site ('ENLYFQ*G') leaving a glycine (G) amino acid residue at the N-termini (referred to as TEVG), which is not well recognised by the N-rule pathway (Varshavsky, 2011).
evidence: This is explained based on known properties of the N-rule pathway cited from Varshavsky, 2011.

claim: Separase cleavage leaves an arginine residue at the N-termini which is a good substrate for N-end rule degradation.
source: In contrast, separase cleavage leaves an arginine (R) residue at the N-termini of the cleaved product ('SVEQGR*R'), which is a good substrate for N-end rule degradation (Varshavsky, 2011).
evidence: This is explained based on known properties of the N-rule pathway cited from Varshavsky, 2011.

claim: Following TEV-induced cleavage, both the N-terminal and C-terminal fragments of Mcd1 are stabilised.
source: Interestingly, Beckouet et al. have shown that following TEV-induced cleavage not only the C-terminal fragment of Mcd1 is stabilised but also the N-terminal (Beckouët et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beckouët et al., 2016.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal Mcd1 fragments were immunoprecipitated by Smc3 after TEV cleavage.
source: Both N- and C-terminal Mcd1 fragments were immunoprecipitated by Smc3 after TEV cleavage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structural integrity of cohesin tripartite complex remains intact after TEV cleavage of its kleisin subunit.
source: Therefore, the structural integrity of cohesin tripartite complex remains intact after TEV cleavage of its kleisin subunit.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The TEV recognition site 'ENLYFQF' (TEVF) leaves a phenylalanine as the N-terminal amino acid after TEV cleavage.
source: We found this to be the case when we used the TEV recognition site 'ENLYFQF' (referred to as TEVF) (Figure 3a). This site leaves a phenylalanine, rather than a glycine, as the N-terminal amino acid after TEV cleavage.
evidence: This is explained in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3a.

claim: N-terminal phenylalanine is a good substrate for N-end rule degradation.
source: Importantly, N-terminal phenylalanine is a good substrate for N-end rule degradation (Varshavsky, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varshavsky, 2011.

claim: Cleavage of TEVG generated stable N- and C-terminal fragments.
source: Cleavage of TEVG generated stable N- and C-terminal fragments as expected (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 3b.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal fragments were rapidly degraded after cleavage on TEVF sites.
source: In contrast, both N- and C-terminal fragments were rapidly degraded after cleavage on TEVF sites (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 3a.

claim: Bulk nuclear separation was observed in both TEVG and TEVF conditions.
source: Bulk nuclear separation was observed in both conditions (Figure 3a–b), with most cells showing full segregation after 120 min of TEV induction (>85% in TEVG and >75% in TEVF).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Figure 3a-b.

claim: More than 85% of cells showed full segregation after 120 min of TEV induction in TEVG condition.
source: Bulk nuclear separation was observed in both conditions (Figure 3a–b), with most cells showing full segregation after 120 min of TEV induction (>85% in TEVG and >75% in TEVF).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data in Figure 3a-b.

claim: More than 75% of cells showed full segregation after 120 min of TEV induction in TEVF condition.
source: Bulk nuclear separation was observed in both conditions (Figure 3a–b), with most cells showing full segregation after 120 min of TEV induction (>85% in TEVG and >75% in TEVF).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Minor delays during anaphase progression were observed in cells with TEVF recognition sites.
source: However, we noticed minor delays during anaphase progression in cells with TEVF recognition sites (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Cells carrying TEVG recognition sites segregated tags correctly with less than 5% missegregation observed.
source: As observed previously, cells carrying TEVG recognition sites segregated tags correctly (with <5% missegregation observed) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data in Figure 3c.

claim: Tag missegregation was observed in 16% of telophases when TEVF recognition sites were present on Mcd1.
source: In contrast, tag missegregation was observed in 16% of telophases when TEVF recognition sites were present on Mcd1 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is quantified from microscopy data in Figure 3c.

claim: Degradation of Mcd1 fragments after TEV cleavage affects the fidelity of chromosome segregation but does not severely prevent bulk nuclear separation.
source: These results demonstrate that degradation of Mcd1 fragments after TEV cleavage affects the fidelity of chromosome segregation but, unlike Mcd1 degradation, does not severely prevent bulk nuclear separation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the data in Figure 3.

claim: Significant levels of chromatin-bound Smc3 remained during initial timepoints in TEV-induced anaphases.
source: We observed that significant levels of chromatin-bound Smc3 remained during initial timepoints (Figure 4a; TEV-induced).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data in Figure 4a.

claim: Smc3 was rapidly lost from chromatin in anaphases induced by auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1.
source: In contrast, Smc3 was rapidly lost from chromatin in anaphases induced by auxin-mediated degradation of Mcd1 (Figure 4a; auxin-induced).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data in Figure 4a.

claim: Full-length Mcd1 was not detected in the TEV-cleaved samples collected for Hi-C analysis.
source: Importantly, we did not detect full-length Mcd1 in the TEV-cleaved samples collected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that TEV cleavage was complete.
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A decrease in intrachromosomal contacts structuration with a loss of loops was observed when comparing Cdc20 arrest to Mcd1-TEVG and Mcd1-AID induced anaphases.
source: When we compared the contact maps of individual chromosomes obtained from cells arrested in metaphase using Cdc20 depletion (Figure 4b), to those obtained for Mcd1-TEVG and Mcd1-AID during the induced anaphases, we observed a decrease in intrachromosomal contacts structuration, with a loss of loops (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C contact maps in Figure 4b.

claim: The contact probability as a function of genomic distances showed a reduction of contacts in the 10–50 kb range for Mcd1-TEVG and Mcd1-AID samples compared to Cdc20 arrests.
source: The contact probability (p) as a function of genomic distances of all chromosome arms showed a reduction of contacts in the 10–50 kb range for Mcd1-TEVG and Mcd1-AID samples compared to Cdc20 arrests (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by distance law analysis in Figure 4c.

claim: The reduction in contacts in the 10–50 kb range was significantly more pronounced in Mcd1-AID than in Mcd1-TEVG.
source: Notably, the reduction in Mcd1-AID was significantly more pronounced than in Mcd1-TEVG (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of distance law curves in Figure 4c.

claim: Removal of cohesin from chromatin in Mcd1-AID causes a very pronounced disruption of cohesin-dependent structure that prevents correct chromosome organisation.
source: These results demonstrate that removal of cohesin from chromatin in Mcd1-AID causes a very pronounced disruption of cohesin-dependent structure (Figure 4b–c) that prevent correct chromosome organisation, and thus explain the catastrophic missegregation observed (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Hi-C data in Figure 4 and segregation data in Figure 1.

claim: Chromosome organisation is not fully disrupted when TEV-cleaved, but chromatin-bound, Mcd1 is present.
source: In contrast, chromosome organisation is not fully disrupted when TEV-cleaved, but chromatin-bound, Mcd1 (and cohesin) is present (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is likely to maintain a level of structure (albeit reduced) that allows bulk nuclear segregation (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Hi-C data in Figure 4 and segregation data in Figure 3.

claim: Smc3-GFP signal was observed on segregated nuclei with a clear discrete dot present at the cell poles that colocalised with the spindle pole body protein Spc29.
source: Smc3-GFP signal was observed on segregated nuclei, with a clear discrete dot present at the cell poles that colocalised with the spindle pole body protein Spc29 (Spc29-RedStar2) (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Figure 5a.

claim: Smc3-GFP might be enriched on centromeric regions of telophase chromosomes.
source: This indicates that Smc3-GFP might be enriched on centromeric regions of telophase chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalisation with spindle pole body marker shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The number of Mcd1 binding sites along chromosome arms was very low in telophase arrests, with only a few sites exhibiting levels above background.
source: The number of Mcd1 binding sites along chromosome arms was very low, with only a few sites exhibiting levels above background (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5b.

claim: Mcd1 is enriched around centromere regions in cdc15-2-arrested chromosomes.
source: However, comparison of average MCD1-6HA profiles across CEN sites confirmed that this cohesin subunit is enriched around centromere regions in cdc15-2-arrested chromosomes (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), thus validating our previous cytological observations (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5c.

claim: Inactivation of cohesin in telophase arrests caused decondensation of rDNA signals.
source: Inactivation of cohesin in telophase arrests caused decondensation of rDNA signals (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Figure 7a.

claim: Comparison of the contact maps revealed changes at centromeric regions in telophase cells depleted for cohesin.
source: Comparison of the contact maps revealed changes at centromeric regions in telophase cells depleted for cohesin (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C data in Figure 6b.

claim: On a large scale (above 200 kb), cohesins favour cis contacts between centromeres and their chromosome arms in telophase.
source: On a large scale (above 200 kb), cohesins favour cis contacts between centromeres and their chromosome arms (Figure 6b and c top).
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C analysis in Figure 6b and c.

claim: At short distances (<100 kb), cohesin impedes contacts between centromeres and their flanking regions in telophase.
source: However, this effect is reversed at short distances (<100 kb). Indeed, panels in Figure 6c show that cohesin impedes contacts between centromeres and their ~100 kb flanking regions.
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C analysis in Figure 6c.

claim: Cohesin complexes influence intrachromatid contacts at centromeres in telophase chromosomes.
source: These results demonstrate that cohesin complexes influence intrachromatid contacts at centromeres in telophase chromosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the Hi-C data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The in trans interaction of CEN sequences was reduced in cdc15-as cells with depleted cohesin.
source: Moreover, the in trans interaction of CEN sequences was also reduced in cdc15-as cells with depleted cohesin (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C analysis in Figure 6d.

claim: Inactivating cohesin in telophase reduces centromere clustering of the yeast genome.
source: Therefore, inactivating cohesin in telophase also reduces centromere clustering of the yeast genome.
evidence: This is concluded from the trans-centromere contact data in Figure 6d.

claim: Contacts between CEN12 and the rDNA are decreased when cohesin is depleted in cdc15-arrested cells.
source: In cdc15-arrested cells, condensin-dependent loop bridges the CEN12 and rDNA (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017). In cohesin-depleted cdc15-arrested cells, these contacts are also strongly decreased (Figure 7b, yellow arrow), suggesting that cohesin plays a role in the formation of this structure.
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C data in Figure 7b and comparison to previous work.

claim: Contacts between pre- and post-rDNA regions are increased when the cohesin complex is disrupted in cdc15-arrested cells.
source: Furthermore, contacts between pre- and post-rDNA regions are increased when the cohesin complex is disrupted, suggesting that it promotes the isolation of these regions in cdc15-arrested cells (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown by Hi-C data in Figure 7b.

claim: Cohesin plays an active role in the organisation of specific regions of the genome in telophase-arrested cells.
source: In conclusion, these results further support an active role for cohesin in the organisation of specific regions of the genome in telophase-arrested cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Hi-C data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Cohesin is loaded onto chromosomes by the loader complex Scc2/4 during G1.
source: Cohesin is loaded onto chromosomes by the loader complex Scc2/4 (Ciosk et al., 2000) during G1 and becomes cohesive during DNA replication (Uhlmann and Nasmyth, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciosk et al., 2000 and Uhlmann and Nasmyth, 1998.

claim: Cohesin becomes cohesive during DNA replication.
source: Cohesin is loaded onto chromosomes by the loader complex Scc2/4 (Ciosk et al., 2000) during G1 and becomes cohesive during DNA replication (Uhlmann and Nasmyth, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uhlmann and Nasmyth, 1998.

claim: The cohesive state of cohesin requires the acetylation of Smc3 by the Eco1 acetyl transferase.
source: The cohesive state requires the acetylation of cohesin Smc3 by the Eco1 acetyl transferase to make cohesin refractory to an inhibitory 'anti-establishment' activity dependent on Wapl (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Unal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008 and Unal et al., 2008.

claim: Cleavage of Mcd1 by separase prompts anaphase segregation in yeast.
source: In yeast, cleavage of one of cohesin subunits, Mcd1/Scc1, by the protease separase (Esp1) prompts anaphase segregation (Uhlmann et al., 1999; Uhlmann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uhlmann et al., 1999 and Uhlmann et al., 2000.

claim: Separase activity is blocked by a bound inhibitor named securin (Pds1).
source: Firstly, separase activity is blocked by a bound inhibitor named securin (Pds1) (Ciosk et al., 2000), which is destroyed by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis once cells are ready to enter anaphase (Cohen-Fix et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciosk et al., 2000 and Cohen-Fix et al., 1996.

claim: Securin is destroyed by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis once cells are ready to enter anaphase.
source: Firstly, separase activity is blocked by a bound inhibitor named securin (Pds1) (Ciosk et al., 2000), which is destroyed by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis once cells are ready to enter anaphase (Cohen-Fix et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cohen-Fix et al., 1996.

claim: Separase-mediated cleavage of Mcd1 is primed by Polo-kinase (Cdc5)-dependent phosphorylation of Mcd1 at serines 175 and 268.
source: Secondly, separase-mediated cleavage of Mcd1 is primed by Polo-kinase (Cdc5)-dependent phosphorylation of Mcd1 at serines 175 (S175) and 268 (S268), on the cleavage sites (Alexandru et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alexandru et al., 2001.

claim: Mcd1 cleavage by separase is thought to terminate the function of cohesin on yeast chromosomes at the anaphase onset.
source: At the anaphase onset, Mcd1 cleavage by separase is thought to terminate the function of cohesin on yeast chromosomes (Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: This represents the prevailing view that the manuscript challenges, supported by citation to Nasmyth, 2001.

claim: Cohesin's subunits have been shown to be chromatin-bound during anaphase/telophase.
source: Interestingly, cohesin's subunits have been shown to be chromatin-bound during anaphase/telophase (Renshaw et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 1999), however the functional contribution of this cohesin population has not been studied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Renshaw et al., 2010 and Tanaka et al., 1999.

claim: Condensin and cohesin are mutually exclusive on mammalian chromosomes.
source: Recent studies demonstrate that condensin and cohesin are mutually exclusive on mammalian chromosomes (Abramo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abramo et al., 2019.

claim: From anaphase to cytokinesis, chromosome-bound cohesin appears as condensin comes off mammalian chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, from anaphase to cytokinesis, chromosome-bound cohesin appears as condensin comes off chromosomes (Abramo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abramo et al., 2019.

claim: Chromosome folding in telophase was found to be independent of both condensin and cohesin in mammalian cells.
source: However, chromosome folding in telophase was found to be independent of both condensin and cohesin (Abramo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abramo et al., 2019.

claim: Cohesive cohesin topologically embraces DNA.
source: An important difference between cohesive cohesin and loop extruding complexes lies in the way that these complexes interact with the DNA substrate. While cohesive cohesin topologically embraces DNA (Srinivasan et al., 2018), loop extruding complexes rely on non-topological interactions (Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Srinivasan et al., 2018.

claim: Loop extruding complexes rely on non-topological interactions with DNA.
source: An important difference between cohesive cohesin and loop extruding complexes lies in the way that these complexes interact with the DNA substrate. While cohesive cohesin topologically embraces DNA (Srinivasan et al., 2018), loop extruding complexes rely on non-topological interactions (Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davidson et al., 2019.

claim: Cohesin complexes cleaved by TEV are likely still able to interact non-topologically with the DNA substrate.
source: Therefore, it is likely that cohesin complexes cleaved by TEV are still able to interact non-topologically with the DNA substrate (Figure 7b) and/or can maintain extruded loops.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TEV-cleaved cohesin maintains some structural function.

claim: TEV cleavage has only a modest effect on the loop extrusion (structural) role of cohesin while disrupting the cohesive role.
source: This would explain why TEV cleavage has only a modest effect on the loop extrusion (structural) role of cohesin, while disrupting the cohesive role (that depends on topological association) (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and theoretical considerations.

claim: Auxin-mediated degradation would abolish both topological and non-topological interactions of cohesin.
source: In contrast, auxin-mediated degradation would abolish both topological and non-topological interactions (Figure 7c), which would result in the loss of cohesion but also structure (and compaction) thus generating a situation where unorganised chromatids would fail to efficiently segregate (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that auxin-mediated degradation causes severe segregation defects.

claim: The loss of cohesin-dependent structures on chromosome arms, but not centromeric regions, on cdc15-arrested cells is reminiscent of the pattern reported for the inactivation of the cohesin regulator Pds5.
source: Interestingly, the loss of cohesin-dependent structures on chromosome arms, but not centromeric regions, on cdc15-arrested cells is reminiscent of the pattern reported for the inactivation of the cohesin regulator Pds5 (Costantino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work supported by citation to Costantino et al., 2020.

claim: Pds5 has been shown to restrict loop expansion.
source: Pds5 has been shown to restrict loop expansion (Costantino et al., 2020; Dauban et al., 2020) and therefore Pds5 absence in telophase could potentially explain our observations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Costantino et al., 2020 and Dauban et al., 2020.

claim: Cohesin is necessary for the maintenance of the structure of the rDNA during metaphase through the regulation of condensin localisation.
source: Recent work has shown that cohesin is necessary for the maintenance of the structure of the rDNA during metaphase and that this role is executed through the regulation of condensin localisation (Lamothe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lamothe et al., 2020.

claim: Yeast cohesin plays important roles during segregation, maintaining the looped organisation of segregating chromatids and supporting centromere organisation.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrates that yeast cohesin plays important roles during segregation, possibly after separase cleavage, maintaining the looped organisation of segregating chromatids and supporting centromere organisation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Yeast cohesin has important post-metaphase functions critical for ensuring faithful genome segregation.
source: Therefore, these findings extend the repertoire of cohesin roles on chromosomes, demonstrating that this complex has important post-metaphase functions critical for ensuring faithful genome segregation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
